prompt: In `Shelf`'s output, `static block: [fiction, history]` came before `main starts`. Why?
hint: `main` is a static method of `Shelf`.

choices.text: Static blocks run when the JVM starts, before any class is chosen
choices.why: They run per class, when that class is first used; section 03 shows a class whose block waited until `new Book()`.

choices.text: The class must be initialised before any of its static methods runs
choices.why: Right: running `main` is a use of `Shelf`, so its static initialisers and blocks ran first.

choices.text: The block is written above `main` in the file
choices.why: Position in the file orders static initialisers among themselves, not against `main`.

choices.text: `javac` moved the block into the first line of `main`
choices.why: `javap -p` showed it as its own member, `static {}`, separate from `main`.

prompt: `javap -p Shelf` listed `static {}` and no member for the instance block. Where did the instance block's code go?
hint: It ran before each constructor's own line.

choices.text: Into the class initialiser, next to the static block
choices.why: Then it would have run once; the output showed it twice, once per object.

choices.text: Into `main`, before each `new Shelf`
choices.why: `main` is one method among many callers; the block runs whoever calls the constructor.

choices.text: Into the start of every constructor, after its superclass call
choices.why: Right: the compiler copies instance initialisers and blocks into each constructor, which is why none can skip them.

choices.text: Nowhere: it is interpreted from the source at run time
choices.why: The JVM runs bytecode only; the source is not in the class file.

prompt: A class has two constructors that both need the same five lines of set-up. What does the section recommend over an instance block?
hint: Lesson 13 had one constructor call another.

choices.text: One constructor calling the other with `this(...)`
choices.why: Right: the shared work is then visible in the constructor somebody is reading.

choices.text: A static block, so the set-up runs only once
choices.why: Set-up for each object cannot run once for the class; the objects would share one result.

choices.text: Copying the five lines into both constructors
choices.why: That is two copies to keep in step, which is what both the block and `this(...)` avoid.

prompt: A block of braces inside a class, marked with the keyword `___`, runs once per class rather than once per object.
hint: It is the same keyword lesson 15 put on fields and methods.

prompt: `Book extends Item`, and neither class has been used yet. Put what happens on the first `new Book()` in order.
hint: Classes before objects, superclass before subclass.

prompt: `Order` printed lines numbered 1 to 7 for the first `Book`. How many numbered lines did the second `new Book()` print?
hint: Which steps happen once per class?

prompt: `main: before the first Book` printed before either static block of `Item` or `Book`. What does that show?
hint: When is a class initialised?

choices.text: That `System.out` buffered the static blocks' lines
choices.why: The lines are in the order they were printed; nothing was held back.

choices.text: That `Order`'s static block runs before every other class's
choices.why: `Order` has no static block, and the point is when `Item` and `Book` ran theirs.

choices.text: That a class is initialised the first time it is used, not when the program starts
choices.why: Right: `Item` and `Book` waited until `new Book()` needed them.

choices.text: That static blocks run after `main` returns
choices.why: They ran in the middle of `main`, at the first `new Book()`, and `main` carried on after them.

prompt: You swap `Book`'s field `title = note("5 ...")` and its instance block in the source, so the block is written first. What changes in the output?
hint: Inside one class, which rule decides?

choices.text: Nothing: field initialisers always run before instance blocks
choices.why: There is no such ranking between the two; they run together, in source order.

choices.text: Lines 5 and 6 change places, in both objects
choices.why: Right: initialisers and blocks of one class run in the order they are written.

choices.text: Line 6 moves before line 3, ahead of `Item`'s part
choices.why: `Item`'s part still finishes first; the swap only reorders steps inside `Book`.

choices.text: The compiler refuses a field declared below an instance block
choices.why: Fields and blocks may come in any order; only reading a field before its declaration is restricted.

prompt: `javac Order.java` compiled one file. How many `.class` files did it write, and why?
hint: `ls *.class` listed `Shelf.class` too, from section 02.

choices.text: One, `Order.class`, because a file compiles to one class file
choices.why: The listing had `Book.class` and `Item.class` beside it.

choices.text: Four, one per class plus one for the file itself
choices.why: `Shelf.class` was the fourth, and it belongs to section 02's file.

choices.text: Three, one per class declared in it
choices.why: Right: `Book`, `Item` and `Order`, each initialised separately by the JVM.

prompt: `Trap` printed `Item() sees: null, 0 pages`. Why was `pages` 0 when its declaration says `= 100`?
hint: When does `Book`'s field initialiser run relative to `super()`?

choices.text: Because `int` fields ignore their initialiser when the class has a superclass
choices.why: The initialiser ran; `afterwards` printed 100.

choices.text: Because it runs after `super()` returns, and `Item()` read it before
choices.why: Right: during `Item()` the field still held its default, 0.

choices.text: Because `describe()` in `Item` has its own `pages` field
choices.why: `Item` has no `pages`; the call reached `Book`'s `describe()` and read `Book`'s field.

choices.text: Because `final` on `title` made the whole object read-only during construction
choices.why: `pages` is not `final`, and nothing is read-only during construction; it is simply unset.

prompt: In `Trap`, `Item()` calls `describe()`. Which version runs, and why does that create the problem?
hint: What kind of object is being built?

choices.text: `Item`'s version, because the call is written inside `Item`
choices.why: Then it would have printed `an item`; it printed `null, 0 pages`.

choices.text: `Book`'s, because the object is a `Book`, and its fields are not set yet
choices.why: Right: the override runs before the code that sets the fields it reads.

choices.text: Neither: a constructor cannot call instance methods, so the JVM substitutes defaults
choices.why: It can, and it did; the defaults are the fields' values, not a substitution.

prompt: What does the section give as the rule that avoids the trap?
hint: Which methods can a subclass not replace?

choices.text: Declare every field `final`, so that it can be set only once
choices.why: `title` was `final` and still read `null`.

choices.text: Give every field an initialiser
choices.why: `pages` had one and still read 0.

choices.text: A constructor should not call a method a subclass can override
choices.why: Right: call a `private`, `static` or `final` method, or do the work after construction.

choices.text: Put the subclass's constructor body above the superclass's
choices.why: Java runs the superclass's part first; no arrangement of the source changes that.

prompt: In `Early`, `this.title = title;` comes before `super();`. Why did `Item()` then see the title but still see `0 pages`?
hint: `pages = 100` is not a statement in the constructor.

choices.text: The field initialiser still runs after `super()` returns
choices.why: Right: only what is written above the call moves; step 5 stays where section 03 put it.

choices.text: Code before `super()` may set reference fields but not `int` ones
choices.why: Any field of the object may be assigned there; `pages` simply was not.

choices.text: `Item()` caches the first value it reads and ignores later ones
choices.why: `Item()` caches nothing; it read what the field held at that moment.

choices.text: Java 25 runs field initialisers before constructors only for `final` fields
choices.why: There is no such rule; the order of initialisers is the same for every field.

prompt: Which of these may a Java 25 constructor do before its `super(...)` call? Choose all that apply.
hint: The object is not built yet, so it may be written to and not read.

choices.text: Check an argument and throw an exception
choices.why: Yes: `Early` refused a blank title before `Item` was involved.

choices.text: Assign one of the object's own fields
choices.why: Yes: `this.title = title;` did exactly that.

choices.text: Call one of the object's own instance methods
choices.why: No: the object is not built yet, so its methods may not be called there.

choices.text: Read a field the superclass's constructor sets
choices.why: No: the superclass's constructor has not run, and reading the object is not allowed there.

prompt: `javac --release 21 Early.java` refused the file. What did the message name?
hint: It named the feature and the release that has it.

choices.text: A missing semicolon on line 20
choices.why: Line 20 was the assignment before `super()`, and the message was about the feature, not punctuation.

choices.text: Flexible constructors, which need source 25
choices.why: Right: statements before `super(...)` do not exist on 21.

choices.text: An `IllegalArgumentException` thrown at compile time
choices.why: The exception came when `java Early` ran on 25; the 21 compile never got that far.

prompt: A class `Report` has `static int count = 0;` and a static block `count = 10;` written below it. What is `Report.count` the first time a program reads it?
hint: Static initialisers and blocks run as one, in source order.

choices.text: 0, because the initialiser on the declaration wins
choices.why: The declaration's initialiser runs first, and then the block below it overwrites it.
Right: `count = 0` runs, then the block sets 10, all before the read.

choices.text: It depends on whether an object of `Report` was created first
choices.why: Static fields are initialised once per class, with or without objects.

choices.text: The compiler refuses two assignments to a static field
choices.why: Only a `static final` field may be assigned once; this one is not final.

prompt: A program creates a thousand objects of `Shelf`. How many times does `Shelf`'s static block run?
hint: It belongs to the class.

choices.text: Once
choices.why: Right: static initialisation happens once per class, whatever the number of objects.

choices.text: A thousand times, once per object
choices.why: That is the instance block; the static one ran once in section 02's output.

choices.text: Twice, because `Shelf` has two constructors
choices.why: Constructors decide nothing about static blocks; they belong to objects.

choices.text: Zero times, unless `main` calls it
choices.why: A static block cannot be called; the JVM runs it when the class is first used.

prompt: Match each piece of a class to how often it runs.
hint: Class or object?

pairs.right: once per object, in every constructor
once per object, only for the constructor called

prompt: A `Book` constructor with `this.title = title;` before `super();` compiles on JDK 25. The team's servers run Java 21. What happens when they build with `--release 21`?
hint: Lesson 1's `--release` compiles as that release would.

choices.text: It compiles, and the JVM on the server reorders the statements
choices.why: The refusal happens at compile time; no class file is produced.

choices.text: It compiles, and fails with `UnsupportedClassVersionError` on the server
choices.why: With `--release 21` the version would be 65, which 21 accepts; the problem comes earlier.

choices.text: The compiler refuses it: flexible constructors need source 25
choices.why: Right: that is the transcript at the end of section 04.

choices.text: It compiles with a warning that the order is not guaranteed
choices.why: There is no such warning; it is an error.

prompt: `Item()` calls a `private` method `label()` instead of the overridable `describe()`. Can `Book` change what `Item()` prints?
hint: Can a subclass override a private method?

choices.text: Yes, by declaring its own `label()`
choices.why: A `label()` in `Book` is a different method; `Item()` still calls its own private one.

choices.text: No: `Item()` keeps calling its own, whatever `Book` declares
choices.why: Right: a private method is not inherited, so nothing in `Book` replaces it; that is why the rule names private, static and final methods as safe to call.

choices.text: Only if `Book`'s fields are set before `super()`
choices.why: Setting fields early changes what an override would read, not whether a private method can be replaced.
